title: The kings undone by their senses
hookLine: a handbook for kings says its whole science is victory over the senses
carry: indriya jaya: win your own senses first
tomorrow: crumbs on a pond. who eats first, and who stops them?
last: ASKING IS PART OF THE FAITH.

lines: ONE BUZZ, AND THE BODY TURNS.
cards: A phone buzzes, face down on a nightstand. One buzz, and a whole body turns toward it. A smell from the kitchen does the same, or a song from a passing car.

The Arthashastra, a handbook for kings, names that pull early on. Then it makes a claim that sounds out of place in a book about armies and treasuries. This whole science, it says, is victory over the senses.

teach.h: INDRIYA JAYA: VICTORY OVER THE SENSES.
teach.b: The phrase is indriya jaya, victory over the senses. The text says what it means: the ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue and the nose don't run wild after sound, touch, sight, taste and smell.
Not shut down. Steered. Then it names what has to be given up, and calls them a band of six enemies: desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance and reckless glee.

Hindu teachers still warn of six inner enemies, in a slightly different list. A ruler who can't master them, the book warns, soon perishes, even if he holds the whole earth. Then, instead of a lecture, it tells on kings.
Dandakya, of the Bhoja line, went after a brahmin's daughter, and was destroyed with his kingdom.

Ravana, out of pride, would not give back another man's wife, and lost Lanka and his life. Duryodhana would not give his cousins their share, not even five villages, and got Kurukshetra. The logic is plain.
A ruler who can't govern his anger will govern a kingdom with it.
So the first territory a king has to win is the five doors of his own body. The throne makes bigger whatever sits on it.

how: Hindu teaching on self-mastery speaks of indriya jaya and of six inner enemies, and many Hindus practice it through japa and fasting; in the Arthashastra it is part of a prince's training in its first book, before any word on governing.

o: a hymn sung when a new king is first given his crown
an old law book's list of crimes a king must punish
an old ruling handbook's start: first, master your senses

games.q: who was undone by what — tap the pairs.
p: the band of six inner enemies
ruined by desire for a brahmin's daughter
pride: wouldn't give back another's wife
wouldn't give his cousins their share

s: conquering the senses means shutting them off completely
the text describes the senses not running wild: steered, not destroyed.
the Arthashastra uses Ravana and Duryodhana as warnings
Ravana's pride and Duryodhana's refusal to share sit in its list of kings undone, next to Dandakya.
a big enough kingdom keeps an unmastered ruler safe
the text warns he soon perishes, even if he holds the whole earth.

games.q: you've just been made captain of your team. in week one, a teammate mouths off at you in front of everyone. by this chapter, what's your first move?
o: bench them on the spot, so everyone sees who's in charge.
notice the anger rising, and let it settle before you decide anything.
ignore it for good; a real captain never lets anything bother them.
games.why: the Arthashastra puts the ruler's own anger first on the list of what to master. it doesn't say nothing should bother you; it says don't let the pull do the ruling.

practice: Many Hindus train the senses with japa: one name of God, or a short mantra, repeated slowly, often on a mala of beads. If you pray, choose one name and repeat it softly for the sit.
If you don't, pick one sound around you and follow only that. Either way, when something pulls at you, notice the pull, don't chase it, and come back.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: indriya jaya, victory over the senses, which the book calls the whole of its science.

orig.note: Sanskrit indriyajaya, victory over the senses: the theme of Arthashastra 1.6.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: indriya jaya, win your own senses first. Ravana couldn't. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Arthashastra 1.6 (control of the senses: ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose with sound, touch, form, taste and smell; the whole science is the conquest of the senses; the six to give up; Dandakya, Ravana, Duryodhana among the kings undone)
